newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan Taleban says Pakistani students fighting.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban says Pakistani students fighting.

text.p: The leader of Afghanistan's Taleban movement, Mullah Mohammad Omar, was quoted as saying on Saturday some Pakistani religious students, but no Pakistani troops, were fighting for his purist Islamic militia.

"They come with their own free will and we cannot say no to them," a Pakistan-based Afghan news service, Afghan Islamic Press (AIP), quoted him as saying in an interview at his headquarters in the southern Afghan town of Kandahar.
Afghanistan's opposition northern alliance accuses Pakistan of helping the Taleban with weapons and troops, a charge denied by both Islamabad and the militia.

Omar said no Pakistan army or paramilitiary troops were fighting for Taleban, though some Islamic students had joined what he called a jihad (holy war) waged by his militia, which emerged in 1994 from Islamic shools at Afghan refugees camps in Pakistan and in southern Afghanistan.
"These students from religious schools in Pakistan even do not know how to handle the Kalashnikov (assault rifle)," he said. "The Taleban train them before allowing them to participate in jihad."

Omar said the Taleban, which controls more than two-thirds of Afghanistan including the capital Kabul, would not enter into any peace talks with the opposition alliance unless it released all the militia fighters and officials arrested in the northern town of Mazar-i-Sharif last May.

Hundreds of Taleban fighters and several officials, including then foreign minister Mullah Mohammad Ghous, were arrested when the forces of northern opposition leader General Abdul Malik drove Taleban from Mazar-i-Sharif at the end of May four days after helping it to capture the town.
API quoted Omar as denying rumours that Ghous and other Taleban officials arrested in Mazar-i-Sharif had been killed.
